title: Web Vulnerabilities and Secrets
summary: Defend a React app against XSS, CSRF, and clickjacking, keep sessions and API keys safe, set security headers, and watch your dependencies.
intro: A React app runs on strangers' computers. Every file you ship can be read by anyone who opens the page, and anything one visitor types, like a product review, can end up on another visitor's screen. Attackers use both facts. A script slipped into a review can act as whoever reads it, another site can send requests that carry your shoppers' cookies, and a key left in the bundle can be copied by anyone. This lesson walks through the attacks a frontend developer has to know, using the Trailhead shop: cross-site scripting, where a login should live, cross-site request forgery, the headers that tell the browser to refuse whole kinds of attack, API keys, and the packages your app is built from.

steps.title: Cross-site scripting, and how React escapes
steps.body:
A shop shows things that strangers wrote: reviews, names, questions. If one shopper can write something that runs as code in another shopper's browser, that code can do anything the page can do: read what's on screen, send requests with the victim's login, or show a fake payment form. This is the most common attack on web apps, and React blocks most of it for you. The part that's left is yours. ## What cross-site scripting is **Cross-site scripting**, or **XSS**, is getting your own JavaScript to run on someone else's site, in a visitor's browser. The script runs with the page's own powers, since the browser can't tell it apart from the site's real code. The web course showed the classic way in: a page that puts text into `innerHTML` turns `` into a real image tag, and its `onerror` attribute runs when the broken image fails to load. ## React escapes text for you You saw this in Components, JSX, and Props: when you write `{review.body}` in JSX, React sets it as text, never as HTML. A `<` in the text becomes `<`, the code for a less-than sign that shows on screen instead of starting a tag. So the attacker's tag shows up as harmless characters. The first example below renders the same string three ways and prints the HTML React makes. That's why most React apps never have an XSS bug, even though they show user text everywhere. ```diagram security-and-secrets-xss The same review takes two paths. Only the one that skips escaping runs the attacker's code. ``` In the diagram, the review on the top path goes through JSX braces and comes out as text. The bottom path hands the same string to `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, the browser parses it as HTML, and the `onerror` runs. ## The holes React leaves open React can only protect what goes through JSX the normal way. These are the places it can't: - **`dangerouslySetInnerHTML`** puts a string into the page as HTML, the same as `innerHTML`. The long name is a warning on purpose. Use it only with HTML you made, or HTML you've cleaned. - **URLs.** A link whose `href` starts with `javascript:` runs code when it's clicked. React 19 blocks that in `href` and `src`, as the first example shows, but not in your own code: `window.location.href = url` or `window.open(url)` with a visitor's URL still runs it. Allow only `http:` and `https:` addresses, as `safeUrl` in the second example does. - **Spreading objects you didn't build.** `
` passes every key as a prop, and a key named `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` from a stranger's JSON is HTML again. Pick the fields you need. - **Reaching around React.** A ref that sets `element.innerHTML`, or a library that writes HTML into the page, gets no escaping from React. ## When you have to show HTML Sometimes the HTML is the point. Trailhead's review editor lets shoppers write **bold** and lists, and stores the result as HTML. For that, clean it first with **DOMPurify**, a small library that parses the HTML and keeps only what can't run. It keeps `

`, ``, and links, and drops `

steps.title: Where a login should live
steps.body:
After you log in, every request has to prove it's you. Whatever does that proving is as good as your password while it lasts, so where the app keeps it decides how much one XSS bug can steal.

## Session tokens

When Trailhead checks your email and password, it makes up a long random value, a **session token**, and remembers which user it belongs to. From then on, a request that carries the token counts as yours. A token can travel two ways:

- **In a cookie.** The server sends `Set-Cookie`, and the browser sends the cookie back with every request to that site, without any JavaScript.
- **In a header your code adds.** The app stores the token, often in `localStorage`, and adds an `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header to each request: the bearer token from the Calling APIs From React lesson. Whoever holds one is let in, like a ticket.

## Why localStorage is the risky choice

`localStorage` is readable by every script on the page. That's how your app reads it, and it's also how an XSS bug, or a hacked third-party script, reads it. One line sends the token to the attacker's server, and they can use it from their own computer for as long as it lasts, even after the victim closes the tab.

A cookie with the **HttpOnly** flag, which the web course introduced, can't be read by JavaScript at all. Log in to the shop, open DevTools, and type `document.cookie` in the Console: you get an empty string, because the only cookie is HttpOnly. The browser still sends it with each request. An XSS bug can still make requests while the victim's page is open, but it can't carry the token away, which turns a stolen login into a much smaller problem.

So Trailhead's login answers with a cookie, as the first example shows. The flags work together:

- `HttpOnly`: scripts can't read it.
- `Secure`: it's only sent over HTTPS, so nobody on the network can copy it. Chrome and Firefox make an exception for `localhost`, so it works while you build.
- `SameSite=Lax`: it's left off most requests that other sites start. Part 3 is about why that matters.
- `Max-Age=604800`: it lasts a week, in seconds.

## What the React side does

Almost nothing, which is the point. The app never sees the token. `apiFetch`, the client from the Calling APIs From React lesson, sends `credentials: "include"` so the browser attaches cookies, and the login form posts the email and password and waits for the answer. To know who's logged in, the app asks `GET /v1/me` and keeps the answer in TanStack Query, so the header can say Hi, Sam. Don't store a copy of the user in `localStorage` as proof of login: it's only a cache of what the server said, and the server decides.

## Refresh tokens, in brief

Some systems, especially ones where a separate login service hands out tokens, use two of them. A short-lived **access token**, good for a few minutes, goes with each request. A long-lived **refresh token**, kept in an HttpOnly cookie, is used only to get a new access token when the old one runs out, and each use swaps it for a new one. A stolen access token dies quickly, and a reused refresh token tells the server something is wrong. You'll meet this with login providers. The same rule holds: neither token belongs in `localStorage`.

## Logging out on the server

Logging out has to end the session on the server, not just in the browser. Deleting the cookie in the browser isn't enough if someone already has a copy of the token. Trailhead's `POST /v1/auth/logout` deletes the session and sends back an expired cookie, so the browser drops its copy too. The second example shows the old token failing right after. A good API also ends sessions when the password changes, and lets you log out every device at once.

examples.title: Logging in sets an HttpOnly cookie
examples.prompt: With the shop built and running under `npm run preview`, and the Trailhead API behind it, post Sam's login the way the login form does. `-si` prints the headers along with the body.

The token is only in the `set-cookie` header, a random value with the four flags this part lists, and `Path=/` so it goes with every path on the site. Header names show in lowercase here because Vite's preview server passed the API's answer through. The `Vary: Origin` header comes from that server too. A browser stores this cookie and sends it back on every request to `localhost:4173`, and the app's JavaScript never touches it.

The second command sends the same token by hand, the way an attacker with a copy would, and gets a 401 with the API's problem body: the server deleted the session, so the token means nothing now. steps.title: Cross-site request forgery
steps.body:
Cookies go with every request to their site, even a request that another site started. That's what makes them convenient, and it's what a forged request takes advantage of: the attacker never sees your cookie, they just get your browser to send it.

## How a forged request works

Say Sam is logged in to the shop and, in another tab, opens a page on `evil.example`. That page holds a script that posts a one-star review to the shop's API. The browser sends the request, and without anything stopping it, it attaches Sam's `th_session` cookie, since the request is going to the shop. The API sees a valid session and posts the review as Sam. This is **cross-site request forgery**, or **CSRF**: a request the user never meant to send, made by another site, riding on their cookies.

The **same-origin policy** from the web course doesn't stop it. It stops the evil page from *reading* the answer, but the request was still sent, and for a review, an order, or a change of email address, sending is the damage.

```diagram security-and-secrets-csrf
The evil page's request reaches the API without the session, so it's turned away.
```

## Site and origin

Two words matter here. The **origin**, from the web course, is the scheme, the host, and the port. A **site** is looser: the scheme and the main domain, the part you register, like `trailhead.example`. So `https://shop.trailhead.example` and `https://api.trailhead.example` are different origins but the same site, and `https://evil.example` is another site. Cookie rules work by site.

## SameSite stops most of it

The `SameSite` flag on a cookie says when the browser may send it on a request another site started:

- `Strict`: never. Even following a link from another site to the shop arrives logged out, which feels broken to shoppers.
- `Lax`: only when the user clicks through to the site, a top-level GET. Posts, form submits, and fetches from other sites go without it. This is what Trailhead uses, and what Chrome assumes for a cookie that doesn't say.
- `None`: always, and it requires `Secure`. Only for cookies that must work inside other sites, like an embedded widget.

In the diagram, step 1 is Sam's own login on the shop's tab, which puts the cookie in the browser's cookie jar. In step 2 the evil page posts, and the browser leaves the `Lax` cookie off, since another site started the request. In step 3 the API, seeing no session, answers 401.

## Belt and braces

`SameSite` is a browser rule, and you don't control the browser, so the server checks too:

- **The Origin header.** Browsers add an `Origin` header to every cross-site POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE, and scripts can't fake it. The server keeps a list of origins it trusts and refuses unsafe requests from anywhere else, as the first and second examples show.
- **CSRF tokens.** The server puts a random value in the page or in a cookie the app can read, and the app sends it back in a header. Another site can't read it, so it can't send it. Many backend frameworks do this for you.
- **GET never changes anything.** `Lax` still sends the cookie when someone follows a link to the site, so a `GET /logout` or `GET /cart/clear` could be triggered by any link a shopper clicks on another site. Changes go in POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE, as the web course's table of safe methods says.

JSON APIs get one more barrier for free. A request with `Content-Type: application/json`, or a custom header like Trailhead's `Idempotency-Key`, can't be sent across origins without a **preflight**, the `OPTIONS` request the web course described, and the API's CORS rules turn it down. Attackers know this, which is why the evil page in the third example sends its JSON as `text/plain`. Don't count on the preflight alone: an API that reads the body as JSON whatever its `Content-Type` says, as many do, is still open without the checks above.

Your React code's part is small: send changes with the right methods, and include whatever CSRF token the backend asks for. The defenses themselves live in the cookie and on the server.

examples.title: The API checks where a request came from
examples.prompt: Two pieces of the Trailhead API's server, `trailhead-api/server.mjs`: the list of allowed origins at the top of the file, and the check at the start of the request handler, which runs before any route.
examples.explanation: `unsafe` is true for every method that can change something. For those, if the request has an `Origin` header and it isn't one of the shop's own, the API refuses with 403 before any route runs. A request with no `Origin` at all is let through, since browsers always send one on a cross-site request that changes something. A request without one is coming from a tool like curl, or from another server, and cookies from a victim's browser don't come with those. The list comes from the `TRAILHEAD_ORIGINS` environment variable when it's set, so a deployed API can allow `https://shop.trailhead.example` without a change to the code. The defaults are the shop's dev and preview servers and the Next.js course's app.

examples.title: A request from another site is refused
examples.prompt: Logged in as Sam, with the cookie saved in `cookies.txt` by an earlier `curl -c cookies.txt` login, send a cart change that claims to come from `https://evil.example`.
examples.explanation: The session cookie was valid, and the API still said no: `403 Forbidden`, with a problem body naming the origin it refused. The same command with `Origin: http://localhost:4173`, the shop's own origin, answered `200 OK` with the cart holding one Storm Shell Jacket. curl can put anything in `Origin`, but a browser can't: it always writes the real origin of the page that started the request. So this check catches forged requests from browsers, which are the only ones that carry a victim's cookies.

examples.title: What a forged request looks like
examples.prompt: A page on `evil.example` that tries to post a review as whoever opens it.
examples.code: Loading your prize…
examples.explanation: `credentials: "include"` asks the browser to attach the shop's cookies. `text/plain` is one of the few content types that needs no preflight, so the request goes straight out. The script never reads the answer, and it doesn't need to. Against the shop, it fails twice over. The `th_session` cookie is `SameSite=Lax`, so the browser leaves it off this cross-site POST and the API sees no session. And the request's `Origin` is `https://evil.example`, which the API refuses with 403 before it looks at the session at all.

steps.title: Security headers
steps.body:
Some defenses aren't code in your app at all. They're response headers that tell the browser to refuse whole kinds of attack, so a bug that slips through review still can't do much. They're cheap to add, and an app that sends them is much harder to break.

## Who sets them

Headers are part of the HTTP response, so whatever serves your files sets them: your host, your CDN, or your server. React can't, since it runs after the response has arrived. A Vite app is a folder of static files, so the headers go in your host's settings. Many hosts read a `_headers` file in `dist/` or a JSON config, and a server like nginx has its own config. While you build, Vite's preview server can send them too, which lets you try them before you ship. This is `vite.config.ts` in a fresh Vite project:

```ts
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import { defineConfig } from "vite";

// The headers your host should send, tried locally with `vite preview`.
const securityHeaders = {
  "Content-Security-Policy": [
    "default-src 'self'",
    "script-src 'self'",
    "style-src 'self'",
    "img-src 'self' data:",
    "connect-src 'self'",
    "frame-ancestors 'none'",
    "base-uri 'self'",
    "form-action 'self'",
  ].join("; "),
  "Strict-Transport-Security": "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains",
  "X-Content-Type-Options": "nosniff",
  "Referrer-Policy": "strict-origin-when-cross-origin",
  "Permissions-Policy": "camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()",
};

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [react()],
  preview: { headers: securityHeaders },
});
```

The first example shows them on a response.

## Content Security Policy

A **Content Security Policy**, or **CSP**, is a list of where the page may load things from, sent in the `Content-Security-Policy` header. Each **directive** covers one kind of thing:

- `default-src 'self'`: anything not listed below comes only from your own origin.
- `script-src 'self'`: scripts only from your own files. Inline scripts, the ones written right inside a `<script>` tag in the HTML, are blocked, and so are scripts from any other domain.
- `img-src 'self' data:`: images from your origin, and small images written right into the page as `data:` URLs.
- `connect-src 'self'`: `fetch` may only call your own origin. Add your API's address if it lives somewhere else.

`script-src 'self'` is the one that matters most. An attacker who finds an XSS bug usually injects an inline script or a script tag pointing at their own server, and the browser now refuses both. The second example shows the browser blocking an inline script. A Vite build writes no inline scripts, just `<script type="module" src="/assets/...">`, so a strict policy fits a Vite app with no changes.

When you do need one inline script, CSP allows it by its **hash**, a fingerprint of its exact text, or by a **nonce**, a random value the server puts in both the header and the script tag, new on every response. A nonce needs a server that writes each page as it's requested, which is what the next lesson's server rendering does.

## Report first, then enforce

A strict policy on an existing site can break things you forgot about, like an analytics snippet. So start with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`: the browser reports what it would have blocked, in the console and to an address you choose with the `report-to` directive, but blocks nothing. Fix or allow what shows up, then switch to the enforcing header.

## Clickjacking and frame-ancestors

**Clickjacking** is putting your site, invisible, inside a frame on another page, over a button that says something harmless. The visitor thinks they're clicking Play and actually clicks Place order on your page. `frame-ancestors 'none'` in the CSP tells the browser never to show your page inside another site's frame. Older sites send `X-Frame-Options: DENY` for the same thing.

## The rest of the set

| Header | What it tells the browser |
|---|---|
| `Strict-Transport-Security` | HSTS from the web course: use HTTPS for this site, for as long as `max-age` says |
| `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` | trust the `Content-Type`, and never guess that a file is a script |
| `Referrer-Policy` | how much of the current URL to tell other sites when a link is followed |
| `Permissions-Policy` | which browser features, like the camera or location, the page may ask for |

`nosniff` stops a trick where a file uploaded as an image is loaded as a script. `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, a good `Referrer-Policy`, sends other sites only your origin, never the path and query string, which can hold things like a password reset token. And `Permissions-Policy` with `camera=()` means even an injected script can't ask for the camera.

examples.prompt: With `npm run preview` running in that project, ask for the page. `-I` asks for headers only.
examples.explanation: The config held each header as a name and a value, with the CSP's directives joined by `; ` so each one is easy to read and change on its own line. Every response from the preview server now carries them, after Vite's own headers like `Cache-Control` and `Etag`. Your host's settings would send the same list in production, and you can check them the same way with `curl -sI` against your real address. A free scanner like Mozilla's HTTP Observatory reads them from outside and grades what's missing.

examples.title: An inline script, refused
examples.prompt: The same project, with an inline script in `index.html` of the kind an analytics tool asks you to paste. Opened in Chromium with the policy above, its DevTools console showed this.
examples.explanation: The browser refused to run the inline script and said exactly why: it breaks `script-src 'self'`. The message lists the three ways to allow it: `'unsafe-inline'`, which would let every injected script run too, so never use it, a hash of this exact script, or a nonce. The hash it prints is ready to paste into the policy, and it only allows this exact text, so changing one character blocks it again. The page itself still worked, since the app's own bundle is a file from `'self'`. An injected `<script>` from an XSS bug gets the same refusal, which is the point.

steps.title: API keys and secrets
steps.body:
Everything in `dist/` goes to every visitor. The JavaScript is squeezed and renamed, but it's still text, and anyone can open it in DevTools or download it. So the rule is simple, and teams still break it: nothing secret goes in frontend code.

## Every VITE_ value is public

The Starting a New React Project lesson showed that Vite puts environment variables whose names start with `VITE_` into `import.meta.env`, and that those values are written into the bundle at build time. It also said they're public. Here's what that means. A project has this `.env.local`:

```env
VITE_MAPS_KEY=pk_maps_trailhead_public_1234
VITE_PAYMENTS_SECRET_KEY=sk_live_trailhead_FAKE_9876
DATABASE_PASSWORD=hunter2-FAKE
```

and code that uses the first two:

```tsx
const mapsKey = import.meta.env.VITE_MAPS_KEY;
const paymentsKey = import.meta.env.VITE_PAYMENTS_SECRET_KEY;
```

After `npm run build`, the first example searches `dist/` for all three. The two `VITE_` values are sitting in the JavaScript, and the database password isn't, because Vite never exposes a variable without the prefix. Ignoring `.env.local` in git keeps the file off GitHub, but the build still copies the values into files you hand to every visitor.

## Publishable keys and secret keys

Many services give you two kinds of key, and the difference is exactly this:

- A **publishable key** is made to sit in browser code. It names your account and can do very little: show a map, start a payment form. Payment companies often start them with `pk_`. You limit them further in the service's dashboard, for example to requests from your own domain, so a copied key is useless on another site.
- A **secret key** can do anything your account can: charge cards, refund them, read customer data. These often start with `sk_`. It lives only on a server you control.

So `VITE_MAPS_KEY` is fine. `VITE_PAYMENTS_SECRET_KEY` is a disaster, and the name doesn't make it safe.

## Secret calls go through your backend

When the browser needs something only a secret key can do, it asks your own server, and your server makes the call:

```diagram security-and-secrets-proxy
The secret key only travels on the last hop, from your server to the payment service.
```

In the diagram, the browser calls `POST /v1/orders` on your API with the shopper's session cookie. Your API checks who's asking, works out the price from its own data, never from a number the browser sent, and only then calls the payment service with the secret key from its own environment. The second example is that last call. The browser never sees the key, and your server decides what each shopper is allowed to do with it. The Calling APIs From React lesson made the same point about third-party APIs: call them from the browser only when they allow it with CORS and a publishable key.

## When a key leaks anyway

It happens: a key gets committed, pasted in a chat, or built into a bundle. Deleting the line doesn't fix it. The key is still in git's history, in every copy of every bundle that was ever downloaded, and in any copy an attacker made. Do this instead:

1. **Revoke the key** in the service's dashboard, and make a new one. This is the only step that actually stops it working.
2. Put the new key where it belongs, on the server, and deploy.
3. Check the service's logs for use you don't recognize.

**Secret scanning** catches many leaks before they happen. GitHub scans pushes for the formats of well-known keys and can block a push that holds one, and tools like gitleaks run the same checks on your computer before you commit. Keep `.env.local` in `.gitignore` and commit a `.env.example` with the names and no values, as the Starting a New React Project lesson set up, so teammates know what to fill in without anyone sharing the real values in code.

examples.title: Searching the bundle for secrets
examples.prompt: In the project's folder, after `npm run build`. `-r` searches every file in `dist/`, `-E` allows the `|` that means or, and `-o` prints only what matched.
examples.explanation: Two of the three values came back, both from the one JavaScript file Vite built. The maps key is meant to be there. The payments secret is now public, and anyone who loads the page can copy it out of the file just as `grep` did. The database password didn't show up, because its name has no `VITE_` prefix and the code never used it. Make this search part of your release checks for any secret your project has: if `grep` can find it in `dist/`, so can everyone else.

examples.title: The call that holds the secret, on the server
examples.prompt: `server/payments.ts` in Trailhead's backend, which the orders route calls once it has checked the shopper and the cart. It runs on Node, never in the browser.
examples.explanation: `process.env.PAYMENTS_SECRET_KEY` is read from the server's own environment when the function runs, so the key is never in a file that leaves the server. The amount comes from the server's own total for the cart, never from the browser, since a shopper could change any number the browser sends. `cardToken` is what the payment service's own form in the browser returned, using the publishable key: a one-time stand-in for the card, so the card number itself never touches your server either. Each side holds only the key it should.

steps.title: Dependencies and the supply chain
steps.body:
Most of the code in your bundle isn't yours. A build of the whole shop transforms 327 modules, as the next lesson shows, and nearly all of them come from `node_modules`: React, the router, TanStack Query, zod, and everything they depend on. Each package is code from someone you've never met, and so is each package it pulls in. The **supply chain** is that whole tree, and attacks on it are now a common way into apps.

## npm audit

npm keeps a list of known security problems in published packages, called **advisories**. `npm audit` checks every package in your lockfile against it. The first example runs it in a folder with an old Vite release installed on purpose. Each entry names the package, the versions that are affected, how serious it is, and a link to the advisory, and npm says whether a fix exists. `npm audit fix` updates what it can within the version ranges in your `package.json`, and tells you what needs a bigger upgrade.

Read before you panic. This advisory is about Vite's development server: another website could send requests to it and read the answers while you're building. That matters on your computer, but none of that code ships in `dist/`. `npm audit --omit=dev` checks only the packages your users actually download. Fix both kinds, but fix what ships first.

## Lockfiles and npm ci

`package-lock.json`, from the Starting a New React Project lesson, records the exact version of every package in the tree. Commit it. On a teammate's computer or in CI, `npm ci` installs exactly what the lockfile says, and fails if it doesn't match `package.json`, so nobody gets a newer version that was published an hour ago by whoever took over a package.

## Typosquatting and install scripts

**Typosquatting** is publishing a harmful package under a name one typo away from a popular one, like `raect-router`, and waiting for someone to mistype it. Read the name twice before you install, and check the package's page on npmjs.com: how many people download it each week, and whether its repository is real.

Harmful packages usually do their damage the moment they're installed, with an **install script**: a command a package's `package.json` asks npm to run on your computer during `npm install`, with access to your files and your keys. npm 11.20, the version this course uses, doesn't run a dependency's install scripts unless you approve them. The second example shows npm skipping one and saying so. A few packages have a real need, like `esbuild`, which checks it downloaded the right program for your computer. Review them with `npm install-scripts ls`, and approve each one by name:

```bash
npm install-scripts approve esbuild
```

That records the approval, pinned to the version you reviewed, in an `allowScripts` field in `package.json`:

```json
{ "allowScripts": { "esbuild@0.24.2": true } }
```

Commit it, so the whole team runs the same scripts and a new version has to be approved again.

## Scripts from a CDN

A `<script>` tag that loads a library from a CDN can be changed by whoever controls the CDN. The web course's **Subresource Integrity** fixes that: an `integrity` attribute holds a hash of the exact file, and the browser refuses to run anything else. Packages installed with npm and bundled by Vite don't need it, since the files ship from your own origin.

## Patch React promptly

React itself has bugs too. In December 2025, React published a critical flaw in Server Components, CVE-2025-55182. A **CVE** number is a flaw's ID in the public list of known security problems, so everyone means the same one. This one let an attacker run their own code on the server by sending a crafted request. Fixed versions, 19.0.1, 19.1.2, and 19.2.1, came out the same day, and frameworks that use Server Components, like Next.js, followed with their own. A Vite app that only renders in the browser wasn't affected, but every team on those frameworks had to upgrade at once. Watch for advisories, and let a tool like GitHub's Dependabot or Renovate open a **pull request**, a proposed change that teammates review before it's merged, when a fix is published, so upgrading is a review and a merge instead of a project.

The next lesson moves to the server. It renders the shop's pages there with React itself, which is where Server Components, and that advisory, come from.

examples.title: Auditing an old dependency
examples.prompt: In an empty folder where `npm install -D vite@6.0.0` installed a Vite release from 2024, on purpose.
examples.explanation: Two packages are flagged. `esbuild` is the one with the advisory: its link explains the problem, and `<=0.24.2` says which versions have it. `vite` is listed because it depends on that esbuild, with no advisory of its own here. The summary counts each as one problem, of moderate and high severity. `fix available via npm audit fix` means a newer version inside the allowed range solves it. The command exits with a failure code when it finds anything, so a CI job that runs `npm audit --audit-level=high` fails the build on serious problems.

Severity: moderate
esbuild enables any website to send any requests to the development server and read the response - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-67mh-4wv8-2f99

examples.title: npm skips an install script
examples.prompt: The same install, in the same folder, with npm 11.20.
examples.explanation: npm installed all ten packages but didn't run esbuild's `postinstall` script, the one listed with its command, `node install.js`. It names the script so you can decide, and points at the commands to review and approve it. Vite still works without it, since esbuild's script only double-checks its download. For a package you've never heard of, an install script you didn't expect is a reason to stop and look closer before you approve anything. An approved script runs on the next install.

npm warn install-scripts
npm warn install-scripts Run `npm install-scripts ls` to review, or `npm install-scripts approve <pkg>` to allow.

recap:
- React escapes text in JSX, so XSS gets in only through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, unchecked URLs, spread props, or code that writes HTML itself.
- Clean user HTML with DOMPurify in one component, and let only `http:` and `https:` addresses become links.
- Keep sessions in HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies, never in `localStorage`, and end them on the server at logout.
- `SameSite=Lax`, an Origin check, and GET requests that never change anything stop forged requests.
- CSP, `frame-ancestors`, HSTS, `nosniff`, Referrer-Policy, and Permissions-Policy are headers your host sends, not React.
- Every `VITE_` value is public: secret keys stay on a server, and a leaked key gets revoked, not just deleted.
- Audit dependencies, commit the lockfile, approve install scripts by name, and patch React when an advisory lands.
